evals.prompt:
I need to register a global Infrahub check that detects rack unit collisions
across all racks. The check class is RackUnitCollisionCheck and lives in
checks/rack_unit_collision.py. It runs against a GraphQL query named rack_devices
stored at queries/rack_devices.gql.

Produce ONLY the `.infrahub.yml` snippet that registers both the GraphQL query and
the check definition correctly. Do not include schema, generator, or transform
sections — just queries: and check_definitions:.
evals.expected_output: A `.infrahub.yml` snippet with a `queries:` section listing rack_devices, and a `check_definitions:` entry for the check. The check_definitions entry must NOT contain a `query:` field (Pydantic extra="forbid" rejects it) — the query is bound from the Python class's `query = "rack_devices"` attribute.
expectations: Top-level `queries:` section declares the rack_devices query with file_path queries/rack_devices.gql
`check_definitions:` has an entry for the check with name, file_path, and class_name

The check_definitions entry does NOT contain a `query:` field (this is the central rule — `query` is rejected by the Pydantic model on check_definitions, unlike generator_definitions which does require it)
Only allowed fields appear under check_definitions: name, file_path, class_name, targets, parameters

assertions.name: check-definitions-present
assertions.check: check_definitions has at least one entry

assertions.name: no-query-field-in-check-def
assertions.check: No check_definitions entry contains a `query:` field

assertions.name: only-allowed-fields-in-check-def
assertions.check: check_definitions entries use only name, file_path, class_name, targets, parameters

assertions.name: queries-section-present
assertions.check: Top-level queries: section is present

assertions.name: check-def-required-fields
assertions.check: Each check_definitions entry has name and file_path

at queries/leaf.gql and takes a $device variable. The targets group is leaf_devices,
and the GraphQL $device variable should be bound to the target's name.

Produce ONLY the `.infrahub.yml` snippet that registers both the query and the check
correctly. Do not include schema, generator, or transform sections — just queries:
and check_definitions:.

The check_definitions entry must NOT contain a `query:` field; the query is bound on the Python class via `query = "leaf_config"`.
expectations: Top-level `queries:` section declares leaf_config with file_path queries/leaf.gql
check_definitions entry has name, file_path, class_name, AND targets: leaf_devices AND parameters mapping device to name__value
The check_definitions entry does NOT contain a `query:` field (rejected by Pydantic extra="forbid"; differs from generator_definitions which requires it)

assertions.check: check_definitions entries use only name, file_path, class_name, targets, parameters

evals.prompt:
Write a global check that stops an interface being brought into
service ahead of the device it belongs to. Flag any InfraInterface
whose status is `active` when the device it belongs to has a status
other than `active` or `provisioning`. If an interface's device
cannot be determined, treat that as a violation too. The class is
InterfaceReadinessCheck and the query is named interface_readiness.

Produce two files:
- the GraphQL query, saved to: output.gql
- the Python check class, saved to: output.py
evals.expected_output: A GraphQL query that selects InfraInterface filtered to the active ones and traverses to the owning device to fetch that device's `status { value }` in the same query, plus a Python InfrahubCheck whose validate() unwraps the nested path (guarding each hop against null), reports the readiness violation with log_error, and flags an interface whose device cannot be resolved rather than skipping it.
expectations: The query fetches the owning device's status inside the query via relationship traversal, not just the interface's own fields — a check runs one query with no lazy fetch
The device status is selected inside the device's own node selection set, not merely somewhere after the nested block
validate() reads the nested device status and calls log_error when it is not active or provisioning
Each relationship hop is guarded against null (`or {}`) so a dangling relationship does not crash
An interface whose device cannot be resolved is flagged with log_error, not skipped with a bare continue/return

assertions.name: child-status-filter
assertions.check: Query filters the interface set by an attribute value

assertions.name: traverses-related-node
assertions.check: Query nests into the related device node

assertions.name: fetches-related-attribute-value
assertions.check: The device's own (innermost) node selection set selects a status value, so the parent state is actually fetched

assertions.name: uses-infrahubcheck
assertions.check: Python defines an InfrahubCheck bound to the query

assertions.name: surfaces-violation
assertions.check: validate() reports the violation with log_error

assertions.name: null-safe-traversal
assertions.check: The relationship walk uses a null-guard idiom (`or {}` / `.get(k, {})`)

assertions.name: flags-unresolvable-parent
assertions.check: An unresolvable device is flagged with log_error, not skipped with a bare continue/return

evals.prompt:
Write a check that has to distinguish two different problems on
a `NetVlan`:

1. a `vlan_id` that is present but outside our allowed range, which
   the check can see for itself, and
2. a `vlan_id` the **server** refuses, because the schema has an
   attribute bound on it.

For case 2 the check needs to attempt the write and observe whether
the server accepted it.

My first attempt did this and it passed on everything, including
values I know are rejected:

```python
resp = httpx.post(f"{url}/graphql/{branch}", json={"query": mutation})
if resp.status_code == 200:
    self.log_info(message="accepted")
else:
    self.log_error(message="rejected")
```

Tell me why that passes, and write the correct check.

Save the check to: output.py
Save the `.infrahub.yml` registration to: output.yml
evals.expected_output: An explanation that every executed GraphQL request returns HTTP 200 and puts rejections in the body's `errors` array, so branching on the status code takes the success branch on a rejection and the check fails open. The correct check uses `self.client.execute_graphql`, which raises `GraphQLError` when the response carries errors, catches that specific exception, and calls `log_error`. It must not catch bare `Exception`, which reintroduces fail-open.
expectations: Explains that an executed GraphQL request always returns 200 and carries rejections in the body's errors array
States that branching on the status code fails OPEN: the check passes on the case it exists to catch
Uses self.client.execute_graphql rather than raw httpx or requests
Catches GraphQLError specifically, not bare Exception, and calls log_error in the handler
Handles the locally-detectable out-of-range case separately, since only a server rejection raises
Recommends a test asserting the check FAILS on a known-bad value, since a fail-open check looks identical to a passing one

assertions.name: uses-sdk-execute-graphql
assertions.check: Uses self.client.execute_graphql and no raw HTTP client

assertions.name: no-status-code-branch
assertions.check: Does not branch on an HTTP status code

assertions.name: catches-graphql-error
assertions.check: Catches GraphQLError specifically (not Exception or a bare except) and calls log_error in the handler
